blocks.text: Isaiah 1 does not reject sacrifice, festivals, prayer, or assembly as such. Its accusation is that these acts of worship coexist with bloodshed and a refusal to do justice. The alternative named in verses 16–17 is concrete: cease doing evil, seek justice, help the oppressed, and defend the fatherless and widow. Holiness, justice, and righteousness therefore belong together in this chapter's critique of worship.

The opening verse presents the book as Isaiah son of Amoz's vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of four kings. The received book also contains varied forms of material, including first-person passages, reports about Isaiah, sign actions, and royal narratives. Scholars widely study Isaiah as a book shaped through long collection and editorial development across several historical horizons, though no detailed reconstruction has gained consensus. The usual large divisions of the book can serve as a reading map, but they do not by themselves settle questions about authorship or composition.

The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete witness to all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah. It broadly aligns with the Masoretic tradition while also containing thousands of spelling and substantive differences. Other Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive writings from Qumran likewise show that the book was actively copied and interpreted.

sections.title: A Witness to the Whole Book
